questions.enonce_markdown:
How and why was the CNU created in Cameroon in 1966?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Cameroon National Union (CNU, in French the Union Nationale Camerounaise, UNC) was created on 1 September 1966 at a congress in Bamenda. It united the main political parties of the Federal Republic of Cameroon into a single party, so that Cameroon became a one-party state. This essay explains how the party was formed and why President Ahmadou Ahidjo wanted it.

**1. How the CNU was created**

- **Background of several parties.** After the reunification of 1961 the Federal Republic had an Ahidjo-led Union Camerounaise (UC) in East Cameroon and, in West Cameroon, the Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP) of John Ngu Foncha and the Cameroon People's National Convention (CPNC) of E. M. L. Endeley, with other smaller parties. East Cameroon had also seen opposition from the Bamileke and the UPC rebellion.
- **Ahidjo's gradual campaign for unity.** After 1961 Ahidjo used speeches and meetings to call for the "unification" of the parties, saying that political divisions weakened the new state. From 1962 and 1963 he encouraged the East Cameroon parties to join the UC or to support it, and by 1965 the UC had absorbed or isolated most of its rivals in the East. In 1965 and 1966 negotiations also took place with the leaders of West Cameroon parties.
- **The weakening of the West Cameroon parties.** The KNDP and the CPNC had been in conflict and, from 1965, the KNDP suffered from a leadership crisis (the KNDP crisis) between Foncha and A. N. Jua. This weakened the ability of the KNDP to resist Ahidjo's proposal. The leaders of the CPNC and others in West Cameroon, who also wished to be near power, agreed to merge.
- **The merger and the Bamenda Congress.** In 1966 the UC, KNDP, CPNC and some other parties and groups dissolved themselves and were merged into a single party, the Cameroon National Union, which was proclaimed at the Bamenda Congress on 1 September 1966, with Ahidjo as its president.

**2. Why the CNU was created**

- **To promote national unity.** Ahidjo argued that Cameroon, with many ethnic groups and two different colonial heritages (French and British), needed unity. A single party would help to unify East and West Cameroon and reduce regional and ethnic divisions.
- **To strengthen national development.** The leaders argued that competition between parties wasted energy and resources, and that one party would speed up development and mobilise the population around a common programme.
- **To consolidate Ahidjo's power.** The party gave Ahidjo control of the political system and removed organised opposition. It was a way of ending organised rivalry and the danger of West Cameroon leaders using the federal structure to resist the central government.
- **To control opposition and ensure security.** The government was still dealing with the UPC rebellion, and Ahidjo feared political instability. A single party made it easier to control dissent.
- **African trends and examples.** In the 1960s many new African states (such as Ghana, Guinea, Mali and Tanzania) adopted one-party systems, thought to promote unity and development. Ahidjo followed this trend.
- **Weakness of opposition.** The splits in the West Cameroon parties and the earlier suppression of the UPC made the creation of the single party easy.

**3. Consequences.** The CNU ended the multi-party system and made Cameroon a one-party state, which lasted until 1990. It prepared for the 1972 move from federation to a unitary state, and made it more difficult for West Cameroon, the smaller partner, to keep its own political life.

**Conclusion.** The CNU was formed in 1966 through Ahidjo's persuasion, the weakening of the opposition and the merging of the main parties at Bamenda. It was created to promote national unity and development but also to consolidate the power of the President and to reduce opposition, and it made Cameroon a one-party state.
